children.text: As Obama takes the stage, the PBS commentators compare Obama to a "meteor," referencing his quick rise to national recognition after winning the Illinois Senate seat earlier that year. They also compare him to Adlai Stevenson, a former Illinois Governor and presidential candidate, who delivered a rousing speech at the Democratic National Convention in 1956, also held in Chicago nearly 50 years earlier. Stevenson's 1956 convention speech,

offered an optimistic vision for the United States during the rise of the Cold War and the recent memories of World War II. The commentators make this comparison to Stevenson as the applause dies down before Obama begins, setting expectations that Obama, too, may signify a "new America" amid the Iraq War and recent memories of 9/11.

He spends the first several paragraphs describing his upbringing, mentioning his father as a "poor herdsman," his grandfather as a cook, his maternal grandfather's patriotism in joining Patton's army during WWII. This narration signals to the listener that the speaker comes from a family of honest, purpose, hard work, and loyal to America, establishing what
Aristotle refers to as "ethos" - the character and credibility of the speaker.

In this section, Obama makes intentional use of the first-person plural pronouns like "we" and "our" to emphasize not only his identity as an American, but also to enhance the feeling of inclusivity of everyone in the crowd sharing a joint experience as Americans.

In this section, he uses a series of brief anecdotes about people he's met who are struggling in a variety of different ways to highlight the ways government can do better. He shares the story of workers in Galesburg, Illinois losing their jobs; a woman in East St. Louis who wants further schooling but can't afford it; a veteran in East Moline, Illinois trying to reacclimatize to life after military service. Including the specific names of each person enhances the reliability the speaker and the veracity of his claims. Hearing about specific struggles also enhances the audience's emotions,
employing what Aristotle refers to as "pathos".
